# Draft:Battle of Tuchola (1410)

The Battle of Tuchola took place on November 5, 1410, during the aftermath of the Battle of Grunwald. The battle was part of the larger conflict between the Kingdom of Poland and the Teutonic Order in the Polish–Teutonic War.
Background
After the decisive Polish victory at the Battle of Grunwald, the Teutonic Knights retreated to the Pomorze region in an attempt to regroup and rebuild their forces. In response, Polish King Władysław II Jagiełło sent forces under the command of Piotr Szafraniec to disrupt the Teutonic forces and regain control of Tuchola, which had been seized by the Order.
Battle
The Polish army, numbering around 2,000 to 2,500 cavalry, advanced towards Tuchola from the direction of Koronowo. According to historical accounts by Jan Długosz, part of the Polish forces was hidden in a valley, and 600 archers were sent to feign a retreat in order to lure the Teutonic forces into an ambush.
As the Teutonic Knights pursued, they encountered the main Polish forces, leading to a decisive defeat for the Knights. Many Teutonic soldiers drowned in Lake Zamkowe, which protected the access to the castle. The battle ended in a Polish victory.
Aftermath
Following the battle, the Polish forces withdrew from the area around Tuchola, believing that they had defeated the Teutonic Order. However, one of the Polish knights, Nawir, betrayed his comrades by convincing the commander of the castle, Jan Brzozogłowy, that the Polish forces had been defeated. As a result, the castle was handed back to the Teutonic Order.
Legacy
Today, Tuchola features the Jagiellonian Trail – "Two Swords," a tourist route that links significant locations related to the battle. The route includes several key sites, such as the site of the final skirmishes and the location where the Teutonic knights were forced to retreat.
